name: Rastafari
areas: where preachers first proclaimed Haile Selassie the returned Jesus; Howell's Pinnacle community was in Saint Catherine
the largest Rasta population; 29,026 people identified as Rastas in the 2011 census
Rastafari spread through travel and reggae in the 1970s; Rastas were involved in Grenada's 1979 New Jewel Movement
Jamaican migrants took Rastafari there in the 1960s and 1970s
Caribbean migrants settled from the 1950s; about 5,000 Rastafari in England and Wales in 2001
Caribbean Rastas first arrived in the 1960s; Ghanaian practitioners report social ostracism
a Rasta settlement on land made available through the Ethiopian World Federation; peaked at 2,000
routes: Jamaican migrants take Rastafari to the United States and Canada (1960s and 1970s)
Rastas settle in London among Caribbean migrants (1950s and 1960s)
Rastafari spreads across the eastern Caribbean (1970s)
marks: Street preachers began claiming here that Haile Selassie was the returned Jesus.
Leonard Howell formed a Rasta community here in 1939; the police raided it repeatedly and it closed in 1954.
Thousands of Rastas gathered to see Haile Selassie arrive in April 1966.
A Rasta settlement in Ethiopia, which peaked at about 2,000 people.
The first international assembly of Rastafari groups was held here in 1982.
notes: Haile Selassie is crowned Emperor of Ethiopia in 1930, and Jamaican preachers, beginning in Kingston, proclaim him the returned Jesus; the message spreads among poor communities hit by the Great Depression.
Rastafari grows rapidly in Jamaica and spreads to other Caribbean islands, the United States and Britain; for its first thirty years it is in conflict with Jamaica's authorities.
Jamaican migrants take Rastafari to North America, and a Rasta settlement is established in Shashamane, Ethiopia (1960s).
Haile Selassie visits Jamaica in April 1966, and thousands of Rastas gather to see his arrival.
Through reggae, Rastafari gains visibility abroad and spreads across the eastern Caribbean; it gains respectability in Jamaica.
Haile Selassie dies in 1975, and Bob Marley in 1981; the number of Rastas in Jamaica declines during the 1980s.
The first international assembly of Rastafari groups meets in Toronto (1982), and international networks grow.
There are at least 12,000 Rastas in South Africa; worldwide an estimated 700,000 to 1,000,000 as of 2012.
